meta.notes: Includes detailed explanations, per-option rationales, and MathJax formulas where relevant.

questions.question: Reynolds number is a ratio between which two types of forces?
questions.explanation: Re = (inertial forces) / (viscous forces); predicts laminar vs turbulent regimes.
questions.detailed_explanation: Reynolds number Re = (ρ V L)/μ compares inertia (ρ V² over length scale L) to viscous stresses (μ V/L). At low Re (≪1), viscous forces dominate—flow is creeping; at high Re, inertia dominates and flow may become turbulent. Use $Re = \frac{\rho V L}{\mu}$; in circular pipes transition typically spans $\mathrm{Re}\sim 2\times10^3\text{--}4\times10^3$ depending on disturbances.

rationales.Inertial to viscous: Correct. Re grows with density/speed/length (more inertia) and falls with viscosity (more damping).
rationales.Elastic to inertial: Wrong. Elastic vs inertial is captured by Weissenberg/Deborah numbers in viscoelastic flows, not Re.
rationales.Pressure to gravitational: Wrong. Froude compares inertia to gravity; Euler compares pressure to inertia; neither is Re.
rationales.Surface tension to buoyant: Wrong. Weber compares inertia to surface tension; Bond compares gravity to surface tension.

questions.question: Conservation of mass in a control volume implies:
options: Mass can be created by pressure gradients
Mass entering - mass leaving = rate of accumulation inside
Density remains constant in all flows
correct_answers: Mass entering - mass leaving = rate of accumulation inside
questions.explanation: Continuity: mass is neither created nor destroyed in the system.
questions.detailed_explanation: Integral continuity: $(\dot m_{\text{in}}-\dot m_{\text{out}})=\tfrac{d}{dt}\int_{CV}\!\rho\,dV$. In steady incompressible flow with single inlet/outlet, this reduces to $A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2$; pressure gradients move mass but do not create it.

rationales.Mass entering - mass leaving = rate of a: Correct. That is the general continuity statement.
rationales.Mass can be created by pressure gradient: Wrong. Pressure redistributes mass; it doesn’t create it.
rationales.Velocity must be constant everywhere: Wrong. Continuity relates fluxes, not uniform velocity fields.
rationales.Density remains constant in all flows: Wrong. Constant density is a special case (incompressible).

questions.question: Conservation of linear/angular momentum states that a fluid element will:
options: Accelerate unless acted on by a net force
Continue with the same velocity or rotation unless acted on by a net force or moment
correct_answers: Continue with the same velocity or rotation unless acted on by a net force or moment
questions.explanation: Newton’s second law for fluids; external forces/moments change momentum.
questions.detailed_explanation: Linear/angular momentum are fluid statements of Newton’s laws. Surface forces (pressure/viscous stress) and body forces (gravity) change linear momentum; moments change angular momentum. Integral form: $\tfrac{d}{dt}\int_{CV}\rho\,\mathbf{u}\,dV + \oint \rho\,\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{n})\,dA = \sum \mathbf{F}$.

rationales.Continue with the same velocity or rotat: Correct. Fluid analogue of Newton’s first/second laws.
rationales.Accelerate unless acted on by a net forc: Wrong. Acceleration requires net force, not its absence.
rationales.Always decelerate due to viscosity: Wrong. Viscosity dissipates energy; pressure work can balance it.
rationales.Move only in streamwise direction: Wrong. Secondary flows/vortices are common; direction follows forces.

questions.question: Which region does the right side of the heart pump blood to, and why?
options: Lungs, for CO₂ removal and O₂ uptake
correct_answers: Lungs, for CO₂ removal and O₂ uptake
questions.explanation: The pulmonary circuit exchanges gases at the alveoli.
questions.detailed_explanation: Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → alveolar capillaries where CO₂ diffuses out and O₂ diffuses in. Pulmonary pressures are low to protect alveoli; O₂ equilibration is rapid (~0.25 s at rest), leaving reserve for exercise.

rationales.Lungs, for CO₂ removal and O₂ uptake: Correct. That is the pulmonary circuit’s role.
rationales.Liver, for nutrient storage: Wrong circuit; hepatic portal flow is venous from the gut.
rationales.Kidneys, for filtration: Wrong circuit; renal arteries arise from the aorta (left heart).
rationales.Brain, for thermoregulation: Thermoregulation is systemic; right heart doesn’t uniquely target brain.

questions.question: Cardiac valves open and close primarily due to:
questions.explanation: Valve leaflets are passive; pressure differences drive motion.
questions.detailed_explanation: AV and semilunar valves are passive structures. They open when upstream pressure exceeds downstream pressure and close when reversed. Chordae/papillary muscles prevent prolapse; they do not actively open valves. The aortic valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure.

rationales.Pressure gradients across the valve: Correct. Pressure difference is the primary driver.
rationales.Muscle contraction of valve leaflets: Wrong. Leaflets are connective tissue without contractile myocardium.
rationales.Autonomic neural impulses: Wrong. Autonomics modulate rate/pressure, not leaflets directly.
rationales.Gravity: Wrong. Posture matters, but it’s not the control mechanism.

questions.question: What occurs at the respiratory boundary (alveoli-capillary interface)?
options: O₂ enters blood and CO₂ leaves blood
CO₂ enters blood and O₂ leaves blood
Only O₂ diffuses; CO₂ is convected
correct_answers: O₂ enters blood and CO₂ leaves blood
questions.explanation: Bidirectional diffusion enables gas exchange between air and blood.
questions.detailed_explanation: At the alveolar–capillary membrane (~0.5–1 μm), gases diffuse down partial-pressure gradients (Fick’s law). End-capillary values near sea level: $P_{aO_2}\approx 100\,\text{mmHg}$, $P_{aCO_2}\approx 40\,\text{mmHg}$. Diffusive flux: $\dot n = - D A\,\frac{dC}{dx}$ (or $J=-D\nabla C$).

rationales.CO₂ enters blood and O₂ leaves blood: Wrong; that occurs in tissues, not lungs.
rationales.No gas exchange occurs here: Wrong. This is precisely where exchange occurs.

questions.question: Synovial fluid lubricates joints primarily because it is:
options: Secreted into the joint space and continuously pumped
Stored in cartilage and squeezed out during motion, then reabsorbed
A non-Newtonian gas trapped in cavities
Generated by muscle metabolism during exercise
correct_answers: Stored in cartilage and squeezed out during motion, then reabsorbed
questions.explanation: Poroviscoelastic cartilage acts like a sponge: exudes lubricant in motion, re-imbibes at rest.
questions.detailed_explanation: Articular cartilage is poroviscoelastic. Under load/motion, interstitial fluid pressurizes and is expressed (weeping/poroelastic lubrication), reducing contact and friction. During rest, fluid re-enters by imbibition. Boundary lubrication (lubricin/hyaluronan) and hydrodynamic/squeeze-film regimes also contribute.

rationales.Secreted into the joint space and contin: Wrong. Synovium secretes fluid, but there is no continuous pump.
rationales.A non-Newtonian gas trapped in cavities: Wrong. Synovial fluid is a liquid with shear-thinning behavior.
rationales.Generated by muscle metabolism during ex: Wrong. Muscles don’t generate synovial fluid.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of titanium for implants?
options: High corrosion resistance via oxide layer
questions.explanation: Ti’s modulus is closer to bone than steel but not identical.
questions.detailed_explanation: Titanium (cp-Ti/Ti-6Al-4V) forms a stable TiO₂ passive film (corrosion resistance), is biocompatible, and supports osseointegration. It is non-ferromagnetic and MRI-compatible. Young’s modulus (~100–110 GPa) is still well above cortical bone (~15–25 GPa), so stress shielding can occur—‘identical to bone’ is false.

rationales.Young’s modulus identical to bone: Correct choice as NOT an advantage; modulus is not identical to bone.
rationales.High corrosion resistance via oxide laye: Advantage. Passive film protects in vivo.
rationales.Non-magnetic behavior: Advantage. Safe in MRI with minimal artifact.

questions.question: In volume-based CFD, 'mesh independence' means:
options: The solver does not use a mesh at all
Refining or rearranging the mesh no longer changes results significantly
Results depend strongly on element count
correct_answers: Refining or rearranging the mesh no longer changes results significantly
questions.explanation: After grid refinement, solution converges; further changes yield negligible differences.
questions.detailed_explanation: Mesh independence means QoIs (pressure drop, wall shear, drag, etc.) change negligibly with further refinement/redistribution. Procedure: perform grid-refinement and quantify discretization error (e.g., Richardson extrapolation/Grid Convergence Index). This is verification of numerical adequacy; validation compares with experiments/ground truth.

rationales.The solver does not use a mesh at all: Wrong. That would be meshless methods.
rationales.Mesh elements are always cubes: Wrong. Tet/hex/prism/poly cells exist; shape is not the criterion.
rationales.Results depend strongly on element count: Wrong. Strong dependence indicates non-converged mesh.

questions.question: Main function of red blood cells (erythrocytes)?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin binds O₂; RBCs also carry CO₂ as bicarbonate/carbamino compounds.
questions.detailed_explanation: RBCs transport O₂ via hemoglobin (cooperative binding → sigmoidal saturation curve) and facilitate CO₂ carriage: ~5–10% dissolved, ~20–30% carbaminohemoglobin, majority as bicarbonate via carbonic anhydrase. They lack nuclei/mitochondria to maximize Hb and avoid consuming carried O₂.

rationales.Hormone delivery: Wrong. Hormones circulate in plasma/binding proteins.

questions.question: Main function of white blood cells (leukocytes)?
options: Immune defense and removal of foreign particles
correct_answers: Immune defense and removal of foreign particles
questions.explanation: Leukocytes recognize and eliminate pathogens and debris.
questions.detailed_explanation: Leukocytes (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes/macrophages, eosinophils, basophils) detect, neutralize, and clear pathogens and debris. Innate cells provide rapid responses; adaptive lymphocytes confer specificity and memory. They orchestrate inflammation via cytokines/chemotaxis.

rationales.Thermoregulation: Wrong. Not a primary WBC function.
rationales.Lipid transport: Wrong. Lipoproteins in plasma do that.

questions.question: Main function of platelets (thrombocytes)?
questions.explanation: Platelets aggregate and activate coagulation to limit blood loss.
questions.detailed_explanation: Platelets adhere (via vWF/GPIb) to exposed subendothelium, activate (ADP/TXA₂ release), and aggregate (GPIIb/IIIa–fibrinogen bridges) to form a primary plug; coagulation forms fibrin to stabilize the clot. They derive from megakaryocytes and are anucleate.

rationales.Osmotic regulation: Wrong. Albumin drives colloid osmotic pressure.

questions.question: Compared to an inviscid Newtonian fluid, blood’s velocity profile in a vessel is blunter mainly because:
options: Blood is shear-thickening with no yield stress
Blood is shear-thinning and exhibits an apparent yield stress
correct_answers: Blood is shear-thinning and exhibits an apparent yield stress
questions.explanation: At higher shear rates viscosity drops; central region moves as a plug due to yield-like behavior.
questions.detailed_explanation: Whole blood is shear-thinning and shows an apparent yield stress at low shear (Casson/Herschel–Bulkley). RBC aggregation/deformation create a blunter core and a cell-depleted layer near the wall, lowering effective viscosity. Model form: $\tau=\tau_y+k\,\dot\gamma^{\,n}$ with $n<1$.

rationales.Blood is shear-thinning and exhibits an: Correct. Non-Newtonian features flatten the profile.
rationales.No-slip boundary condition is absent: Wrong. No-slip generally holds in vessels.

questions.question: Given fluid columns with densities 1200 kg/m³, 1000 kg/m³, and 800 kg/m³ as in the figure, what is the pressure at point a?
questions.detailed_explanation: Hydrostatics: $p=p_0+\rho g h$. In connected columns, pressures at the same elevation must match. Walk from a reference surface (~101.3 kPa), adding $\rho g\,\Delta h$ when going downward and subtracting when rising, switching ρ per fluid. The net sum to point a gives ≈103 kPa.

rationales.~103 kPa: Correct. Matches the net hydrostatic sum across the multi-fluid manometer.
rationales.~95 kPa: Too low; would require a larger net rise than present.
rationales.~110 kPa: Too high; would require larger effective ρ·h downward.

questions.question: At 30 m depth breathing 20% O₂, is the O₂ partial pressure safe for prolonged exposure (threshold 60 kPa)?
questions.detailed_explanation: Absolute pressure at 30 m seawater ≈ 1 atm + (1025·9.81·30)/101300 ≈ 3.9–4.0 atm (≈395–400 kPa). Partial pressure: $P_{O_2}=F_{O_2} P_{abs} \approx 0.20\times 395\,\text{kPa}\approx 79\,\text{kPa}$. Long-duration limits target ≤~60 kPa O₂ to reduce toxicity; ~79 kPa exceeds that.

rationales.Safe; ≈ 60 kPa: Below computed PO₂; not applicable here.
rationales.Unsafe; ≈ 120 kPa: Too high for this depth and fraction.

questions.question: For a unidirectional composite with Vf=0.1 (fiber), Ef=100 GPa, Em=3 GPa (parallel to fibers), the effective E is:
questions.explanation: Rule of mixtures: E = Vf*Ef + Vm*Em = 0.1*100 + 0.9*3 = 12.7 GPa.
questions.detailed_explanation: Longitudinal (iso-strain) rule of mixtures: $E_{\parallel}=V_f E_f + V_m E_m$, with $V_m=1-V_f$. Here $0.1\cdot 100 + 0.9\cdot 3 = 10 + 2.7 = 12.7\,\text{GPa}$. Transverse (iso-stress) would be much lower.

rationales.12.7 GPa: Correct from the longitudinal rule of mixtures.

questions.question: Continuity: Water enters a 5 cm radius inlet at 1.5 m/s and exits a 4 cm radius outlet. What is v_out?
questions.detailed_explanation: Incompressible continuity: $Q=A V$ with $A=\pi r^2$. Thus $V_{out}=V_{in}\,(A_{in}/A_{out})=1.5\,(0.05^2/0.04^2)\approx 2.34\,\text{m·s}^{-1}$.

rationales.1.2 m/s: Wrong direction; smaller outlet area increases velocity.
rationales.3.75 m/s: Too high; would need a much smaller outlet radius.

questions.question: With p_in=105 kPa, p_out=101.3 kPa and speeds from Q5, what is Δz (inlet minus outlet elevation)?
questions.explanation: Bernoulli with ρ=1000 kg/m³ gives Δz ≈ 0.212 m.
questions.detailed_explanation: Bernoulli (steady, inviscid, incompressible, along a streamline): $\tfrac{p}{\rho g}+\tfrac{V^2}{2g}+z=\text{const}$. Rearrange for $\Delta z = z_{in}-z_{out} = \tfrac{p_{out}-p_{in}}{\rho g} + \tfrac{V_{out}^2 - V_{in}^2}{2g}$. Insert $p_{in}=105\,\text{kPa}$, $p_{out}=101.3\,\text{kPa}$, $\rho=1000$, $V_{in}=1.5$, $V_{out}=2.34$: $(101300-105000)/(1000\cdot 9.81)\approx -0.377\,\text{m}$; $(5.48-2.25)/(19.62)\approx 0.165\,\text{m}$; sum $\approx -0.212\,\text{m}$ (magnitude ~0.21 m).

rationales.~0.21 m: Correct magnitude from Bernoulli with given values.
rationales.~0.05 m: Too small; underestimates the pressure term.
rationales.~1.0 m: Way too large for the given Δp and speeds.

questions.question: You want the balloon to expand by 1.0 L at 103 kPa and 20°C; air exhaled is at 37°C and 101 kPa. How much air do you exhale?
questions.explanation: Combined gas law gives V1 ≈ 1.079 L to obtain 1.0 L at target conditions.
questions.detailed_explanation: Combined gas law: $\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$. Exhaled air: $T_1=310\,\text{K}$, $P_1=101\,\text{kPa}$; balloon: $T_2=293\,\text{K}$, $P_2=103\,\text{kPa}$; desired $V_2=1.00\,\text{L}$. Then $V_1=\frac{P_2 V_2 T_1}{T_2 P_1}\approx \frac{103\cdot 1.00\cdot 310}{293\cdot 101}\approx 1.079\,\text{L}$ → ~1.08 L.

rationales.1.08 L: Correct from the combined gas law with given temperatures and pressures.
rationales.1.00 L: Only true if temperature and pressure were identical.
